In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new therapeutic approaches to cancer.
the development of monoclonal antibodies (MoAbs) that can be used in radioimmunotherapy for the treatment of human cancer.
the development of a radioimmunotherapy for non-Hodgkin's lymphoma using the murine anti-CD37 monoclonal antibody MB-1 and the murine anti-B1 monoclonal antibody.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the results presented herein suggest that RIT of human lymphoma using pan-B-cell MoAb targeting can produce a specific antitumor effect that is dominated by either antibody-dependent cellular cytolytic activity (with an isotype capable of mediating this activity) or antibody-specific targeted radiation (with an isotope incapable of mediating this cytotoxicity), depending on the isotype of the MoAb used.
the anti-B1 treatment was more effective than the anti-B1 control, and that the anti-B2 treatment was more effective that the anti-B3 control.
the anti-B1 antibody is a better choice for RIT than MB-1, but that the latter may still have a role in RIT if the antibody can be modified to increase its cytotoxicity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that the use of 131I-anti-B1 in a nude mouse model for lymphoma xenografted with Raji Burkitt’s lymphoma cells is effective in producing a reduction in tumor size in vivo.
we found that the anti-B1 MoAb, but not MB-1, could mediate antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxcity in vitro.
131I-labelling of a murine monoclonal antibody to CD37, MB1, produced an antibody specific targeted radiation effect in Raji xenografts in nude mice.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to separate the effects of radiation and antibody in vivo, and that the radiation dose is the dominant factor in the efficacy of RIT.
it is important to use isotype-matched controls in the design and interpretation of clinical trials of RIT.
the use of an antibody that is not capable of mediating antibody dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) is more likely to show a radiation dose effect.
